segments.en: Deep in the highlands, a drumbeat starts, and then another, and another. Dancers in feathered headdresses of red, yellow and emerald green step forward, their faces painted, and the ground seems to shake beneath them.

This is a sing-sing, a gathering of song and dance, and in Papua New Guinea there are more ways of celebrating than you could count. Every clan has its own costumes, its own songs and its own stories.

It is one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth, with more than eight hundred languages. To understand one another, many people use Tok Pisin, a lively language that grew out of English and Pacific words.
In Tok Pisin, thank you is tenkyu, and a warm hello is gude. You might also hear wantok, which means one talk, a person who speaks your language and will always look out for you.

Many families still live in villages, growing sweet potatoes, taro and bananas in gardens cut into steep hillsides. Pigs are highly valued and are given as gifts at weddings and other important events.
For a feast, food is cooked in a mumu, an earth oven where meat and vegetables are wrapped in banana leaves and placed on hot stones in a pit, then covered and left to steam.
In the forests live birds of paradise, with trailing plumes and extraordinary courtship dances. One appears on the national flag, golden against a red sky, above the stars of the Southern Cross.
Along the Sepik River, villages build tall spirit houses called haus tambaran, and carvers create masks and figures that are admired all over the world.
All over the country, women loop colourful string bags called bilum, carried hanging from the forehead, full of vegetables, shopping, or sometimes even a sleeping baby.
Port Moresby, the capital, lies on the southern coast. Out in the islands, there are coral reefs, active volcanoes near Rabaul, and quiet beaches shaded by coconut palms.
Rugby league is the great passion here, and when the national team, the Kumuls, take the field, it seems as if the whole country is watching.
At the Goroka and Mount Hagen shows, groups from all over the highlands come together in their finest bilas, their traditional decorations, and the colour and sound are unforgettable.
Before you go, listen to the rain drumming on the rainforest canopy. Then sail south across the Torres Strait, where Australia is only a short journey away.
